posts.caption: At #Goalkeepers2030, I spoke with Archbishop Vicenzo Paglia about how people and relationships must remain at the center of how we use AI.

Progress doesn’t happen on its own. It happens because the world invests in and prioritizes it. If we can combine increased generosity with the smart use of AI, there’s no limit to the progress we can make.

The Gates Foundation is joining a coalition of organizations to help nearly 3.4 billion people whose languages are underrepresented in AI. posts.caption:
As companies grow, the founder cannot be the source of every good idea. And probably should not be.

You need simple systems that allow curiosity to travel across teams, functions, and geographies.

For us, sometimes that is as basic as an open document, a few minutes every week, and one important rule: don’t judge an idea too quickly.

Innovation does not always need a complicated process.

Sometimes it just needs fewer barriers.

Ambition is rarely limited by the size of the goal. More often, it’s the small habits around it.

A little less discipline, a little more comparison, a little impatience, and even the biggest goal can remain just that: a goal.

Most ambitious goals don’t fail because they were too ambitious. They fail because the everyday habits needed to support them never quite show up.

Sometimes the best advice makes more sense when you read it backwards.

If you had asked me a few years ago how to win in life, I would have said work harder.

But my journey taught me something different.

Winning is not about being harsh, loud or ruthless. It’s about being clear, consistent and kind even when it’s hard.

It’s about understanding that no one is going to want your growth as much as you do. You have to show up for yourself every single day.

It’s about realizing that your title doesn’t define you, your work does. And if you make something with heart, it will always find its way to the right people.

I am still learning, still figuring it out. But these 5 things changed how I look at growth and life.

Sharing it here because I know someone out there needs to hear this today.

Burnout is rarely announced. It usually appears gradually in the form of silence, detachment, and a team that no longer feels connected to the outcome.

As a founder, I believe it is my responsibility to notice that shift before exhaustion becomes the accepted way of working. A team cannot do its best work when it is only trying to get through the week.

It’s not just me; before investing, most investors want to understand whether the business becomes stronger as it grows or simply more expensive to operate.

The right numbers help them see beyond the headline growth. They reveal the quality of the business, the discipline of the founder, and whether the company has the foundations to build something enduring

Today, I’m very proud to share an exciting next chapter for @sirclecollection 

From my first conversations with @riteshagar there was an immediate connection. Ritesh is a special human and an incredible entrepreneur, and we quickly discovered a shared mindset and ambition.

Today, we’re announcing our partnership with Sunday PropTech, backed by PRISM, to accelerate the international growth of Sircle Collection.

What excites me most is how naturally our strengths complement each other. Sircle brings brands, creativity and hospitality expertise; Sunday PropTech, backed by PRISM, brings technology, infrastructure, scale and international reach.

I’m incredibly proud of what our teams have built and very excited about what comes next; bringing Sircle and our brands to more hotels, cities and communities around the world.

Ritesh, looking forward to building this next chapter together! @sirhotels @maxbrownhotels @aterre

A glamorous idea does not automatically make a strong company, and an ordinary idea does not limit how large a company can become.

Give me a founder who understands the customer deeply, executes with discipline, and can improve a familiar industry year after year. That may sound “boring” in a pitch, but it can become a remarkably valuable business.

Investing in the right opportunity starts with looking beyond what the market is today.

For us, that means looking at where hospitality is heading, the demand shaping extended stay, and the kind of product and operating model that can capture that opportunity.

That’s the thinking behind Studio 6 Plus. Built for what’s next in extended stay.

Link in bio to know more.

When I meet a founder, I am not looking for someone who has never failed, changed direction, or been caught without an answer.

I look for self-awareness. Are they learning from failure? Are they willing to follow the customer rather than defend their ego? Can they admit what they still need to figure out?

The signal matters, but the thinking behind it matters more.

I want more people to travel, see new places, experience different cultures, and discover parts of the world they may have only heard about. But if tourism is going to keep growing, we have to prepare for that growth too. 

That means better infrastructure, more skilled talent, thoughtful city policies, and hotels that are ready for the next generation of travellers. The future of tourism is not just about getting more people to travel. It is about making sure destinations are ready to welcome them well.

Tourism is a huge positive for cities. It creates jobs, supports local businesses, and brings people and cultures closer. But when tourism grows rapidly, cities also have to deal with the pressure that comes with it. I don’t think the answer is less tourism. 

The answer is better-managed tourism, with clear rules around what works for visitors, residents, and the industry. The best outcomes will come when all three have a seat at the table.

I probably didn’t realise it then, but some of my earliest lessons about hospitality came long before I ever thought of starting a company. 

Our family holidays were often pilgrimages, and staying with relatives was simply what families like ours did. They were kind enough to host us, but I still remember wishing we had the option to stay somewhere independently. That small childhood thought stayed somewhere in the back of my mind. 

Years later, when I started OYO, I could see the same problem at a much larger scale: millions of people wanted to travel, but a reliable and affordable stay was not always within reach. OYO became a business, of course. But the idea behind it was personal much before it became commercial.

Honestly, still speechless over this. I cannot believe that at age 44, one week after a 100k race, five months post-injury…that this happened. An entire marathon at a mile pace that starts with a 7! A Boston Qualifying time AT BOSTON! And to do this with my son here with me! OMFG!!! 

Have been working so so hard, and it doesn’t always come together on race day. But when it does…there’s no feeling quite like it.

Fastest Known Time on the Baja Sur 135km Trail! 

On March 6, I attempted the Fastest Known Time (FKT) for Mexico’s 135km Baja Sur Trail across the entire Baja Sur Peninsula. 

82 miles from the Pacific Ocean → Sea of Cortez.
13,000 feet of elevation.
One absolutely savage mountain section from miles 17–34 that climbed 6,000 feet in just 6 miles — including three straight miles at 30% grade in peak heat.
40 miles through night under the moon and stars.
One 5-minute dirt nap after mile 60.
And a sunrise at mile 70 that made the entire effort feel almost spiritual.

My first “comeback” ultra distance after injury. 

Final result?
24 hours, 53 minutes, 10 seconds

Which was the Fastest Known Time for ANYONE on that trail, male or female

FKTs are different than races.
There are no set aid stations.
No course marshals or race directors. 
You build the entire attempt yourself — the logistics, the pacing plan, the fueling, the documentation — and then you go see if your body and mind can execute it.

This one took an incredible team.
Huge gratitude to my pacers — including my ride or die @dr.joelipsky, absolute rock star running partner Ben Thompson, and the incredible @joecorcione who agreed to run 60+ miles of the effort with me, including the insane mountain climb section, on just a few days of notice. These incredible friends rotated through the desert with me for nearly 25 straight hours, alongside a support vehicle leapfrogging us for lightning-fast resupplies.

The mountain was the hardest trail I’ve ever climbed.
But running under the stars, seeing the desert sunrise, laughing through the pain cave and finishing on the beach after running across an entire peninsula?

That’s a feeling I’ll carry for a long time.

Lots more to come including more incredible footage, but wanted to share as soon as we completed the attempt successfully. Thank you to Ben and the Joes 😂 Thank you to @linsanityz @mounttocoast (should be renamed coast to mount to coast?) Thank you to the amazing @drmeganroche who saved my quads and my fueling strategy. Miami, you were beautiful, painful, chaotic, insane and amazing in all the best ways. The race was an adventure-style checkpoint race, where you didn’t learn the course until you were in it, and you got the directions for each checkpoint in real time. I ran over bridges, around islands, through neighborhoods, and navigated crowded touristy areas. All in hot and crazy humid Florida weather. 

When @joecorcione said he thought I was capable of running a ~20 hour 100 miler time (roughly a 12 minute mile, including stops) I didn’t quite believe him. My PR for the distance is 23:30 which I just ran in July. 

But 20 hours and 24 minutes later, I crossed the finish line as first place female and third place overall, averaging a 12:03 pace after running 100 miles non-stop, with very few breaks, except to change water logged sneakers a few times or use the restroom.

But a race performance like this doesn’t happen without an absolute incredible crew firing on all cylinders. @murrclurr_ is beyond amazing as a crew chief. @joecorcione and Ben Thompson did an unreal job pacing, helping me navigate the course, and pushing me through peak heat. And my husband @btworetzky absolutely crushed it on my crew out there. This race was just as challenging to crew, as to run, and I was in absolute awe of my team the entire time. 

Special shoutout to @dr.joelipsky who wasn’t physically there with us, but absolutely was in spirit, and helped me crush one of the best training blocks I’ve ever had. And to @pinknoelephants who has become an essential part of the team and @quietgratefullife who surprised me out on the course. 

My legs are sore and my body is a bit wrecked, but my heart is so happy and I feel beyond proud and excited for what lies beyond.

The past few days have seen some fun milestones!!

🍊 My 1,000th OrangeTheory class! 
I walked into OTF almost four years ago with no clue how that gym would change my life. Countless 6am classes, some of my closest friendships, big goals dreamt & done, and a whole lot of life lived under those orange lights. Naturally, we celebrated the only reasonable way: a 6am toga party. 

🔥 My son’s new 5k PR! I got to run side by side in matching outfits with my son Simi, as he dug so deep and set a new PR on the exact same course where he last set a PR at this distance, two years ago. Super proud mom. Even prouder of the fact that Simi has poured so much heart into his Team for Kids charity fundraiser for his upcoming Disney race. 

🏙️ Bronx 10 Mile: My first ever 10 mile race! The course was so fun - starting and ending at Yankee Stadium. And my first time racing for @jhenwood72’s @henwoodshounds team. Held a 7:24/mile pace and felt so good doing it. Even better was getting to run bonus warm-up and cool down miles to and from the race with Sydney.

Three milestones that look totally different on paper. My first race for a new team. My kid’s PR. A hilariously large number of 6am workouts.

But really, they’re all the same thing. Keep showing up for yourself and find people who make showing up wildly fun. 

Oh. And always, always wear a costume.

The pressure to perform. To lead. To win. To keep going when things get hard. And, as someone who thinks running 100 miles is a reasonable recreational activity 😂, I’m endlessly fascinated by the question:

What makes some people extraordinarily good under pressure?

I’m SO excited to share that after twelve years of my business talk radio show on SiriusXM, our show is back better than ever for our thirteenth year with a whole new relaunch:

🎙️ UNDER PRESSURE with Randi Zuckerberg

I’ll be sitting down with some of the mentally toughest people I know across business, sports & life—not just to hear what they accomplished, but also their failures, fears & moments they wanted to quit…but didn’t. What secret mental fortitude did they access to push beyond what most other people could not?

Because I want us to steal their secrets. 

And I could not imagine a more extraordinary first guest than Ali Feller. 💙 @aliontherun1 - Ali is one of the toughest, most resilient, badass women I have had the pleasure of getting to know - and through it all, has the most infectious smile, energy, and spirit.

I found a new puzzle and I’m having so much fun being a beginner at it!

Rather than get increasingly good at surviving ridiculously long distances, @dr.joelipsky and I schemed that maybe this should be the summer of seeing how fast I could learn to run the 50k distance. It’s a deceiving distance - on the surface, it’s “only five miles longer than the marathon” - but in reality, those five extra miles feel like a whole entire marathon in themselves. 

Earlier in the summer, I ran a time trial 50k on a bike path, with Joe supporting me on the bike, and finished in 4:44 (a 9:07/mile pace). I loved it — but finished knowing there was a lot more there.

So we started playing around with new workouts, different types of long runs, and how to get the most out of tired legs.

Today I went back to the exact same bike path, exact same starting time, Joe supporting me, and ran another 50K.

4:31:46
8:43/mile pace

More than 12 minutes faster.

I’m 44 years old. When I got back into running at age 41, my one mile PR was 9:30. It absolutely blows my mind that today I ran 31.1 miles at a pace almost a full minute a mile faster than that. I love that I have run almost every distance imaginable (and some distances that seem unimaginable!) and there are STILL so many completely new things to learn. 

One of my favorite things about endurance sports is that you never reach a point where someone hands you a certificate saying, “Congratulations, you’re done. You have now discovered your full potential.”

You just get to keep being entrepreneurial, keep finding new puzzles to solve, and keep pushing the limits.

I’m well aware that running 100+ mile races as a 44 year old mom of three is….well…unusual. 

I know most people have no desire to do it.
I know there are WAY easier ways to see beautiful places.
I know that eating quesadillas out of a folding chair at 2am while someone patches up 15 blisters on your feet is not everyone’s idea of a good time.

But one of my favorite things about getting older is that I no longer need the things I love to make sense to anybody else.

I love short races, too! You’ll find me at tons of them! But I don’t run ultramarathons simply because I haven’t learned to “just be ok with fewer miles.” I run them because I genuinely love what happens when the distance get long: the adventures, the places, the empowering confidence, the problem-solving, the ridiculousness of it all - and most importantly, the new tiny corners of myself that I discover along the way. 

If your thing is 18 holes, go live your best life!
If your thing is knitting, knit the WHOLE DAMN BLANKET!
And if your thing is running absurdly long distances while eating gas station snacks…well, I’ll probably see you out there! 

Just please don’t expect me to make the thing that I love smaller, just because you could never see yourself enjoying it. We’re old enough to know what brings us joy. We don’t have to shrink it into something other people understand.

Today, @BarackObama, @MichelleObama and @BChesky, Airbnb co-founder and CEO, welcomed the fifth cohort of Voyager Scholarship recipients: 100 college juniors preparing for careers in public service.

The 2026–2028 class represents 39 states and territories and 68 colleges and universities. Sixty-one percent of the cohort are first-generation college students, bringing even more perspectives and lived experiences to the Voyager community.

Their work spans some of today’s most pressing challenges, from resilient infrastructure for island communities and water quality in the Great Lakes to accessibility policy for the Deaf community and the use of artificial intelligence in clinical care. Others are exploring graphic design as a tool for community engagement, first-time voter participation, food access in urban neighborhoods, and economic opportunity in rural and Appalachian communities.

“Every year, this scholarship reminds Michelle, Brian, and me that there is no shortage of young people ready to take on hard problems,” said President Obama. “This year’s Voyagers come from small towns and big cities, from islands in the Pacific and neighborhoods here on the South Side. They are working on housing, health care, clean water, and public safety, and most of them started that work long before anyone offered to pay for it. We’re proud to help them keep going.”

At the heart of the Voyager Scholarship is a shared belief that experiencing communities and cultures around the world can deepen understanding, build empathy, and prepare the next generation to create meaningful change.
Along with scholarship support, summer travel funding, and personalized career coaching, Voyagers participate in monthly virtual sessions where they sharpen their vision for a career in public service, strengthen their bridge-building skills, and build relationships with one another.

We can’t wait to see where their journeys take them. Join us in welcoming the newest class of Voyagers in the comments!

I’ve been sitting with this title for a long time. No Country for Mothers.

Say it out loud. You already know it’s true.

American moms have asked ourselves for years why motherhood is so hard in this country. Why we’re exhausted. Why we’re blamed. Why nothing ever seems to change no matter how loud we get. So we did something about it. 

We teamed up with @culturehousemedia and we made a film to find out. 

No Country for Mothers is the documentary I wish existed before I became a mom. It’s the reckoning we deserve. And it’s finally here.

Watch the trailer, then comment MOTHERS below and I’ll send everything straight to your DMs. Screenings are coming to a city near you.
Let’s go. 🎬

Gender relations in the U.S. are broken — this is how I think we can fix it. 

It starts by recognizing the big con: that progress is a zero-sum game. Here’s what I mean:

“They’ve built a world where men and women don’t talk to each other, don’t see each other, don’t trust each other. Disconnection isn’t just the consequence — it’s the goal. Because if we don’t see each other, we won’t stand up for each other… The story that you’ve been told: that power is a pie and you got to fight for your slice, that’s a lie. They got you so busy fighting a gender war to keep you from fighting a class war.”

Congrats again to @harvey_mudd’s class of 2025!

Yesterday, I asked @RealDonaldTrump what he would do to solve America’s #childcare crisis. His response? Incomprehensible at best. At worst? Outrageously offensive to the millions of families drowning in childcare costs.

It shouldn’t take an economics degree to understand this: parents cannot work without childcare.

Which makes childcare an economic issue.

But we have spent decades treating it like a personal problem mothers are supposed to solve alone. And then blame them for stepping back from work instead of asking why the system failed them.

#NoCountryforMothers breaks down the economic pressures forcing women into impossible choices and why that policy failure keeps getting pinned on moms.

Of course nobody could name the most powerful woman in tech. We spent four years dismantling the rooms she’d be standing in.

Read the full investigation from @laurengoode at @WIRED, link in my stories.

Motherhood is still the unfinished business of feminism.

Too many mothers are still forced to choose between their families and economic security — without paid leave, affordable childcare, or the support to make either choice sustainable.

We made #NoCountryforMothers to show what happens when motherhood is left out of the fight for equality, and why that has to change.

The film is not available to stream because it is meant to be watched in community. Find a screening near you (or host one yourself!) at the link in bio.

We screened part of No Country for Mothers at the Columbia University Mailman School of Public Health (@columbiapublichealth), and the conversation afterward was exactly why we made this film.

Huge thank you to Lauren Houghton, who organized the evening on behalf of Mailman and joined me on the panel. Her Free Time 4 Wellness study is showing what every mom already knows: give a mother free childcare and she finally has time for her own health. Lauren is turning that into data a policymaker or a CEO can’t ignore, and I’m so grateful she brought us into her work.

And thank you to Emmy Liss, who leads NYC’s Mayor’s Office of Child Care and Early Childhood Education (@nycchildcare) and is one of the people delivering universal childcare in this city. Listening to her talk about what it actually takes to deliver reminded me that this is completely possible when leaders decide to do it.

Many thanks also to Dean Jonathan Mermin for welcoming us, Randi Hutter Epstein for moderating, and the whole Mailman team for a beautiful night.

In 2024, the Surgeon General called parental stress an urgent public health issue. How can we expect mothers to take care of their own health when we make it so hard to take care of their kids? Research, policy, and advocacy each get us part of the way there. Put them in the same room and you start to see how we actually win.

You can’t stream No Country for Mothers anywhere. The only way to see it is at a community screening, so find one near you or host your own at the 🔗. 

#NoCountryForMothers

This is one of the most dangerous times to be an American woman.

And still, we are being told that women are the reason men are struggling. That women have too much power. That pulling women back is the way forward.

They want us fighting each other, but #NoCountryforMothers is about seeing through that distraction, and coming together to demand the support mothers, fathers, and families deserve.

Today I join so many others in honoring the life and mourning the loss of an icon — Gloria Steinem.

I grew up admiring Gloria from afar, and later had the extraordinary honor of getting to know her. Her commitment to equality and justice for all knew no bounds and was matched only by her generosity to her friends.

As I was writing Lean In, she offered to read my drafts. She did — and sent me edits line by line — with the most generous note possible: “This is your book and my notes are just suggestions.”

That was Gloria. She spent her life making room for other women to find and use their voices, and somehow still had the ability to make you feel like yours was the one that mattered most. She didn’t just fight for a movement — she built people up, one relationship, one march, one magazine, and even one joke at a time. And she did that for nearly six decades — and right until the very end.

The world is quieter today for the loss of her voice. But so many of us carry a piece of what she gave us — so many of us know that all of our work stands on her shoulders.

Rest in power, Gloria.

Today is American Business Women’s Day, and I keep thinking about how recently women could be required to have a man’s signature to get a business loan.

Some states still required women to have a husband or other male relative co-sign a business loan until 1988?! What?! That was only 12 years before I started @spanx.

The progress came in steps. In 1974, the Equal Credit Opportunity Act made it illegal to deny women credit or require a male co-signer simply because they were women. Then, in 1988, the Women’s Business Ownership Act eliminated state laws requiring a husband or other male relative to co-sign a woman’s business loan - and expanded support for women entrepreneurs.

Not that long ago, a woman’s ability to access credit could depend on a man’s signature instead of her own ambition and ability to build. 🤯

Think of all the businesses, ideas, and inventions that may not have had the chance to exist before then.

I’m a big believer that the more women-owned businesses we have in this world, the better. ❤️

posts.caption: My hope for the future? That every woman—no matter who she is or where she lives—can step into her full power because she’s able to get the care she needs.

If you want proof that our health systems overlook women, just look at menopause. It affects half the population, yet it remains poorly understood and drastically underfunded, leaving women without the care and relief they need. 
 
In The New York Times, I share why I’m directing new funding to raise the standard of care for menopause and perimenopause—and what it will take to unlock a menopause revolution. Read the full piece at the link in my bio.

Unlocking women’s power changes everything.
 
In our homes. 
In our workplaces. 
In our communities. 
In the rooms where laws are passed. 
And at the tables where decisions are made.

“You didn’t get listened to, but here’s how to be listened to more.” That’s the message women get constantly — and I don’t think we say the other part enough: you should be listened to. 

That should be where we start, not where we’re negotiating to.

Full report linked in my bio.

#parenting #emilyoster #data #evidencebacked #melindafrenchgates

“I want every good thing for this child before I have another.” A mom named Marianne told me that when I was in Kenya in 2011, and it’s stuck with me ever since. Every parent, no matter where they live, wants the chance to give their children the best possible start in life. On #WorldContraceptionDay, let’s remember that starts with something fundamental: the ability to decide whether and when to have children.

A journalist raising questions about lung cancer rates in women. A doctor who nearly became a maternal mortality statistic. A columnist shining a spotlight on menopause.  
 
These leaders are using their voices and platforms to highlight the distinct health challenges half the population faces.  
 
Today I’m sharing eight key voices for information and inspiration. I’d love to hear what you’d add to this list. Who and what have you been listening to, reading, or watching lately to learn more about women’s health?

I’ve heard from women all over the world how important it is to be able to decide for themselves whether and when to have children.

That’s why it’s essential that they have access to contraceptives and reliable information about their options. Their health and their families’ futures depend on it. #WorldContraceptionDay

When we think about the stakes in healthcare, we tend to think of them in terms of life and death, being sick or being healthy. The conversation is about your physical well-being and maybe your mental health — and it pretty much stops there.

But your health impacts so much more, especially for women, a new survey from Gallup and Pivotal, a philanthropic group founded by Melinda French Gates, shows.

“Women are often taught to put themselves last and minimize their own needs,” Melinda wrote to Vox in an email. “They don’t always have time to care for themselves because they’re so busy caring for others. And they might not be able to afford childcare or home health support for their aging parents. Our survey showed one in six women delayed healthcare because of their responsibilities caring for their family members. For Black women it’s one in five, and Hispanic women one in four. Too many women are facing an uphill road to even just get to a doctor’s office.” 

“It’s possible to make it easier for people to balance healthcare and family responsibilities — but it’s going to take action from many angles. That’s exactly why I invest in both women’s health and in caregiving, and I’d encourage more philanthropists to do the same.”

Read more about why we need to invest more in women’s health — and how to accomplish it — at the link in our bio.

📸: Courtesy of Pivotal Ventures

More than 50% of U.S. women have had a negative experience seeking healthcare in the last five years. And 42% said their health has limited their careers.  
 
When women can’t get the care they need, it impacts every aspect of their lives. 
 
@pivotaldotcom partnered with @gallup to conduct one of the most expansive surveys on women’s health and opportunity ever fielded.  
What we found was that, for women, barriers to care too often become barriers to opportunity.  
 
Learn more about our findings on Pivotal.com

From hot flashes to night sweats, menopause comes with a long list of things women are told to brace for. Far less discussed is what menopause can cost a woman at work.

A major new survey from @pivotaldotcom, @melindafrenchgates, and Gallup quantifies that cost—and data shared exclusively with Marie Claire shows just how unevenly it falls. Women with the least financial cushion are absorbing the steepest career costs.

Tap the link in our bio to read more.

Women’s health is too important for any one group to tackle alone. That’s why I’m calling on business leaders, policymakers, philanthropists, care providers, and advocates to use their influence to improve women’s health.

That afternoon, I was riding down the West Side Highway when I spotted a car dealership and told the taxi driver to pull over. I walked into the showroom and pointed to the smallest car, figuring it would be the cheapest.

“What’s that cute brown car in the corner?”

“A 911 Carrera.”

“That’s the brand?”

So touching to see @VirginAtlantic’s new plane paying tribute to my wonderful wife, Joan. 
 
Joan was part of the Virgin Atlantic story from the very beginning. Did you know that @Virgin once imagined the iPod, but we made it into an April Fool’s joke!

In 1986, we announced the Virgin Music Box: a machine that could store music and let you call up any song you wanted. We thought it was so farfetched it would pass as a ‘gotcha’ moment. How wrong we were!

Years later, the world caught up with the idea, and I remember thinking: we should have built the bloody thing. The moral of the story is that when an idea feels slightly ridiculous, don’t dismiss it too quickly.

Sometimes the ridiculous ideas are a not-so-distant future...

We give ourselves health checks. Our planet deserves one too.

Today, while in New York for Climate Week, I joined the Planetary Guardians and the brilliant Professor Johan Rockström to launch the 2026 Planetary Health Check, an annual scientific assessment of the systems that keep our Earth healthy.

The news is confronting. Seven of the planet’s nine safety boundaries have now been crossed, and all seven are moving in the wrong direction.

This isn’t some distant problem happening to somebody else. We feel it through hotter days, rising food prices, polluted air, floods, fires and droughts. It affects all of us.

But it’s not all doom and gloom - there are real reasons for hope. Solar power is doubling roughly every three years. One in four new cars sold worldwide is electric. And investment in clean energy is now nearly twice that going into fossil fuels.

The solutions are here. Now we need to use them at speed and scale to get our planet back into a safe space.

I want my grandchildren, and yours, to inherit a world every bit as beautiful as the one we’ve been lucky enough to enjoy.

Read the Planetary Health Check, share its findings and add your name to the call for planetary health to sit at the heart of global decision-making. This issue isn’t bigger than any of us, because every one of us can help.
